topicName: TempDB Design, Contention, and Best Practices
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"TempDB Design, Contention, and Best Practices in Microsoft SQL Server"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"TempDB is a global resource available to all connected users of an instance of SQL Server. It is used to hold temporary user objects, internal objects created by the database engine, and row versions generated by data modification transactions. Improper configuration of TempDB is one of the leading causes of performance bottlenecks in high-concurrency enterprise environments."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding TempDB Workloads"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before optimizing TempDB, it is crucial to understand what types of objects reside within it. TempDB workloads generally fall into three categories:"},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"User Objects: Explicitly created temporary tables (#temp, ##temp), table variables, and table-valued parameters."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Internal Objects: Spooling operations for queries (such as hash joins and sorts), service broker, XML variables, and cursors."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Version Store: Page versions generated by features like Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI), Snapshot Isolation, Online Index Operations, and Triggers."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Identifying TempDB Contention"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Allocation contention occurs when multiple sessions concurrently attempt to allocate pages in TempDB. This manifests as high wait times on latches such as PAGELATCH_UP, specifically on pages like 2:1:1 (GAM), 2:1:2 (SGAM), and pages within system allocation bitmaps. You can diagnose allocation contention using dynamic management views."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"SELECT session_id, wait_type, wait_duration_ms, resource_description FROM sys.dm_os_tasks WHERE wait_type LIKE 'PAGELATCH_%' AND resource_description LIKE '2:%';"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practice 1: Multiple Data Files"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"To mitigate allocation contention, TempDB should be configured with multiple data files. A common rule of thumb is to create one data file per logical CPU core, up to a maximum of 8 files. If contention persists, you can increase the number of files in multiples of 4."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"ALTER DATABASE tempdb MODIFY FILE (NAME = tempdev, SIZE = 8GB, FILEGROWTH = 1GB);\nALTER DATABASE tempdb ADD FILE (NAME = tempdev2, SIZE = 8GB, FILEGROWTH = 1GB);"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practice 2: Equal File Sizing and Autrowth"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"All TempDB data files must be configured with the exact same initial size and identical autogrowth increments. SQL Server uses a proportional fill algorithm to write to TempDB files. If files are of unequal size, the proportional fill will favor the larger files, rendering the multi-file setup ineffective and creating localized bottlenecks."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practice 3: Trace Flag 1118 (or SQL Server 2016+ Equivalent)"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Trace Flag 1118 forces SQL Server to allocate full extents (8 pages at once) for user and internal objects in TempDB instead of mixed page allocations. This drastically reduces contention on SGAM pages. Note that in SQL Server 2016 and later versions, this behavior is enabled by default for all databases via the ALTER DATABASE setting MIXED_PAGE_ALLOCATION."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practice 4: Storage Configuration and Placement"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"TempDB activity is intensive and continuous. Place TempDB data and log files on the fastest available storage subsystem (such as dedicated NVMe or SSD drives). Furthermore, isolate the TempDB transaction log onto its own separate disk spindle or high-performance volume away from the TempDB data files to minimize disk I/O contention."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practice 5: Pre-sizing TempDB"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Allowing TempDB to rely on default autogrowth settings during peak business hours can cause severe query performance degradation due to synchronous zero-initialization delays. Always pre-size TempDB data and log files to a value that comfortably handles peak operational workloads, avoiding frequent autogrowth events."}]
